items.stem: Write a Python class CircularQueue(size) with enqueue(x) (return False if full), dequeue() (return None if empty), is_empty() and is_full(), using a fixed-size list and front, rear and count attributes.
items.markingKey:
Model answer (Python; an equivalent Java solution is equally acceptable):
class CircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, size):
        self.size = size
        self.arr = [None] * size
        self.front, self.rear, self.count = 0, -1, 0
    def is_empty(self):
        return self.count == 0
    def is_full(self):
        return self.count == self.size
    def enqueue(self, x):
        if self.is_full():
            return False
        self.rear = (self.rear + 1) % self.size
        self.arr[self.rear] = x
        self.count += 1
        return True
    def dequeue(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            return None
        x = self.arr[self.front]
        self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.size
        self.count -= 1
        return x
Marks: correct headers/parameters; correct logic and boundary handling; correct return values/output. Tested with:
q = CircularQueue(3)
assert q.enqueue(1) and q.enqueue(2) and q.enqueue(3) and not q.enqueue(4)
assert q.dequeue() == 1
assert q.enqueue(4)
assert [q.dequeue(), q.dequeue(), q.dequeue(), q.dequeue()] == [2, 3, 4, None]

items.answer: In a linear array queue the rear only moves forward, so freed cells at the front are wasted (or items must be shifted); a circular queue wraps the pointers around to reuse those cells.
